title: MC2-03248
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): They are appealing the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dismissing their refugee protection claim on the grounds that they did not rebut the presumption that Colombia offers adequate protection to its citizens.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the male appellant), XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the female appellant), XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX (the minor appellants) are citizens of Colombia. They allege that they fear being found and killed in their country by people who profit from corruption in the health care system that the female appellant helped to expose for an information program run by her brother-in-law.

They are appealing the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dismissing their refugee protection claim on the grounds that they did not rebut the presumption that Colombia offers adequate protection to its citizens.
The determinative issues in this appeal are the principle of natural justice and procedural fairness, credibility and state protection.

I dismiss the appeal. Although I do not agree with all of the RPD's conclusions, I consider that its determination is correct and that the appellants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection. BACKGROUND The Refugee Protection Division's decision

The RPD considered that the appellants had not demonstrated that they had made efforts to obtain state protection. It concluded that they had not established, on a preponderance of probabilities, that they had gone to the police station in the municipality of XXXX to file a complaint or that the police had then refused to consider the complaint.

It was of the view that if an attempt to file a complaint had in fact failed, the appellants could still have tried to file a complaint at another police station or with another authority, which they did not do.

The RPD also did not accept that the complaint had been rejected because the appellants were being persecuted by the police at the XXXX station or even by the entire Colombian state. According to the RPD, the female appellant had not demonstrated that she had a profile that would lead to the entire Colombian state's refusal to protect her or that she had made efforts to obtain state protection.
It concluded that the appellants had not rebutted the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence, as they had the burden of doing. The appellants' arguments

The appellants are of the view that there was a breach of procedural fairness because, firstly, the RPD shortened the amount of time they had to prepare and submit their appeal record, by providing the reasons for rejecting their refugee protection claim late. In that regard, the appellants initially received the Notice of Decision and the accompanying reasons belonging to another person on February 17, 2022. They received the reasons for their own refugee protection claim on March 16, 2022.

Secondly, they allege that this one-month delay in notifying them of the reasons justifies an apprehension of bias on the part of the RPD member. They submit that if the reasons had already been prepared on February 17, 2022, it would have only taken a few minutes to properly notify them. They argue that since no one explained to them the reason for the delay, it can be believed that the reasons were not ready on February 17, 2022, and that the outcome of their refugee protection claim was the same as the Notice of Decision in order to maintain a certain consistency in the RPD's reputation, which was already impacted in relation to the other refugee protection claimant whose reasons they received.

The appellants are requesting that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) intervene and correct this error and take the corrective measures that their case merits. They note that the Federal Court has stated that "a 'proceeding' as contemplated by paragraph 166(c) of IRPA is not just the hearing but all that which occurs from the institution of the matter until its final disposition."1

With respect to state protection, the appellants submit that the issue was incorrectly assessed by the RPD, as it did not state, with clear and adequate reasons, how they had failed to discharge their burden of establishing the absence of state protection. They argue that the RPD's conclusions are unintelligible, as there is confusion between state protection and credibility. They submit that there is no justification or explanation as to why the RPD did not believe their testimony.

The appellants add in their memorandum that during the hearing, the interpretation was not continuous, faithful or competent, as the RPD had to ask the interpreter at various times to repeat the translation or provide clarification. They are therefore of the view that the RPD could not rely on what the female appellant may have understood or not understood during the indirect questioning.

The appellants also allege that the RPD incorrectly required evidence corroborating the police complaint, as it relied solely on the lack of such evidence to make an adverse credibility finding2 when the female appellant had testified that she had been unable to file her complaint. In that regard, the female appellant submits in her statement3 that she sought protection from the Colombian state but was humiliated and mistreated, which is why she did not continue to seek state protection.

The appellants add in their memorandum that conclusions such as those issued by the RPD are considered unreasonable by the Federal Court because approaching state authorities is not a precondition to be recognized as a refugee. They claim that they established that they had gone to the police station in XXXX in vain and that it was objectively reasonable not to insist on seeking protection from the Colombian state, which is not able to offer them adequate protection, particularly given the profile of the female appellant, who had experienced government corruption up close and had exposed it.

They state that there was no point in filing a complaint with the national police, the prosecutor's office or any other authority because the agents of persecution have contacts within those organizations due to their political appointments. Referring to the objective evidence,4 they argue that the measures taken by the Colombian state are not working adequately and that corruption remains a major concern. They note that the national police in Colombia have much more work than they can handle, due to a lack of resources,5 and that the profile of people who are provided with protection does not correspond to that of the female appellant.6 Resources are set aside so that some protection can be provided when a person receiving a threat holds a position of leadership or power or is a senior public servant, but not otherwise.7 They are of the view that given the conditions in the country, adequate protection is not available to them in Colombia.
They are requesting that the RAD allow their appeal and recognize them as refugees or persons in need of protection or, alternatively, to refer the matter back to the RPD for re-determination.

In support of their appeal, the appellants submitted the following exhibits: - Exhibit A-1: Letter from the RPD, XXXX XXXX, 20228 - Exhibit A-2: Statement by the female appellant's brother-in-law, XXXX XXXX, 20229 - Exhibit A-3: News article on a corrupt police officer, February 8, 202210 - Exhibit A-4: News article on a police officer trafficking cocaine, February 21, 202211 - Exhibit A-5: News article on the Colombian electoral campaign, March 19, 202212 - Exhibit A-6: News article on the penitentiary system, March 27, 200213

In accordance with subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), I may accept only evidence that arose after the RPD made its decision or that was not reasonably available at the time of the decision or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented to the RPD before the decision was made.
If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must determine whether the evidence is new, credible and relevant before admitting it.14

The appellants are requesting that the new evidence be admitted because it arose after the rejection of their refugee protection claim and is "capable of proving or disproving a fact that is relevant to the claim for protection".15 They submit that the new evidence is credible, reliable and relevant because their lives and future are at stake and this evidence has a direct impact on the RPD's conclusions concerning state protection.

Exhibit A-1 is the letter from the RPD informing them of a breach of confidentiality, dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2022. The document is credible. The incident arose after the RPD's decision and is relevant to the allegations of a breach of procedural fairness and of impartiality. The document is admitted in evidence.

Exhibit A-2 is the statement by the female appellant's brother-in-law, a journalist with whom she collaborated as a source of information about corruption in the health and education sector. Although he refers primarily to events that occurred during his collaboration with the female appellant, her brother-in-law also discusses events that occurred in XXXX 2022, after the RPD's decision. These events are therefore new and relevant to the situation in Colombia and seem credible. The document is admitted in evidence.

The articles in exhibits A-3 and A-4 refer to corrupt police officers. The article in Exhibit A-5 describes corruption in the electoral process. Exhibit A-6 illustrates corruption in the Colombian judicial system. These documents describe the various levels affected by corruption. They are submitted in response to the RPD's reasons, were published after the RPD's decision, seem to be from credible sources and are relevant to the situation in Colombia. They are admitted in evidence.
My role is to consider all the evidence and determine whether the RPD's decision is correct.16

As a result, I have conducted my own independent analysis of the record to determine whether the RPD erred, based on the arguments presented by the appellants in their appeal memorandum. To that end, I considered all the evidence on the record and listened to the recording of the virtual hearing held by the RPD on February 3, 2022. Principle of natural justice and procedural fairness

I cannot accept the appellants' claims that the RPD's administrative errors constitute a breach of procedural fairness with respect to the preparation of this appeal. While it is highly regrettable that the appellants had to wait a month before receiving the RPD's reasons for rejecting their refugee protection claim and that there was a breach of confidentiality for another claimant, the appellants had possible remedies at their disposal to address the lack of time to properly prepare their appeal,17 remedies they did not make use of.

The appellants do not explain how that shorter period prevented them from fully and fairly presenting their position for this appeal. They were nonetheless able to submit new evidence in support of their appeal, again within the statutory time limits, without needing to submit an application under the Rules for submitting documents not previously provided.18 I conclude that the appellants therefore have not established that their right to a fair proceeding has been violated.

It is important to note that the appellants were informed of the outcome of their refugee protection claim on February 17, 2022. According to the Notice from the person who is the subject of the appeal, they filed their appeal on March 7, 2022,19 well before receiving the RPD's reasons, which were signed and issued by the RPD on February 7, 2022.20

In her statement21 attached to the appeal, the female appellant requests a new hearing before a differently constituted panel, fearing that the RPD member who heard her case was unable to show the required partiality because of an administrative error resulting in the delay before sending the reasons for his decision. The female appellant argues that the member was not impartial because he was forced to issue adverse reasons in keeping with the notice of a negative decision sent a month earlier.

Such allegations are serious and cannot be made lightly. They cannot rest on mere suspicion, pure conjecture, insinuations or mere impressions of a claimant or his or her counsel. They must be supported by material evidence demonstrating conduct that derogates from the standard.22

The allegations that the reasons were written only after the Notice of Decision was sent, to comply with it in order to preserve the RPD's reputation, are mere conjecture and no material evidence was submitted in that respect by the appellants. The delays caused by administrative errors are not sufficient to suggest a reasonable apprehension of bias on the part of the member.
It is one thing for the appellants to be dissatisfied with the outcome of their refugee protection claim. However, there is nothing to support their suspicions of bias on the part of the RPD member.

With respect to the interpretation issues raised by the appellants, listening to the recording of the hearing shows that their counsel and the member both understood Spanish.23 At one specific moment, the member asked the interpreter to validate the month in the date of an incident about which the female appellant was testifying, which was done, and the date provided by the female appellant was correctly translated. That error, so to speak, did not have any repercussions on the reasons rendered by the RPD and, if there had been other determinative translation errors during the hearing, it was up to the appellants' counsel to raise them immediately. I am also of the view that any other error in translation would have been raised by the member, as he did for the date error.
This leads me to conclude that there was no breach of the principle of natural justice or procedural fairness in the handling of this claim. Credibility

At the hearing, the RPD raised many concerns about the female appellant's allegations, including about her participation in the fight against corruption. However, it was of the view that the determinative issue24 in this case was state protection, while rejecting the allegation that the appellants had tried to file a complaint on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019, with the police in the municipality of XXXX.

The RPD rejected that allegation, referring to the objective documentary evidence25 concerning the procedure for filing a complaint. It also criticized the appellants for not inquiring with the various authorities in order to file a complaint and not submitting independent evidence that could have also helped support their complaint with the authorities.

The female appellant stated in her Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form) and in her testimony that she went to the police station on XXXX XXXX, 2019, and that her complaint could not be dealt with because nothing had happened to her and she had not identified the people following her. She also stated that she contacted the protection service on XXXX XXXX, 2019, to see if she would be offered protection. Although the purpose of that call was instead to confirm that the people looking for her were in fact agents of their service, I am of the view that if protection had been possible for the reported event, the female appellant could have been informed of that during that call, which was not the case.

It is important to note that when a refugee protection claimant swears to the truth of their allegations, this creates a presumption that those allegations are true unless there is reason to doubt their truthfulness.26 In this case, the RPD did not note any inconsistencies in the appellants' testimony. In my view, and based on the objective documentary evidence raised by the RPD, it is entirely possible that the appellants went to the police station as they state and that their complaint was rejected. In that regard, the objective evidence states that unfounded complaints will not be accepted.27 What the appellants described is therefore corroborated by the objective evidence. They explained that since they had not identified the people following them and because nothing had happened to them, the police refused to accept their complaint.

In addition, I am of the view that there was no basis for a negative inference concerning the failure to produce documents corroborating the attempted complaint. I agree with the RPD that the photograph28 of a police officer in no way establishes that the appellants went to the station on XXXX XXXX, 2019, to file a complaint. However, the RPD did not provide legitimate reasons for doubting the appellants' credibility, and since they did not file a complaint, they could not produce such a document as evidence. The RPD could not reject on that basis the appellants' testimony.

As a result, I conclude that the RPD erred with respect to credibility, as there was no reason to doubt the appellants' testimony about the attempt to file a complaint at the police station. State protection

In the absence of a complete breakdown of the state apparatus, there is a presumption that state protection is available.29 The onus is on the refugee protection claimant to rebut that presumption.30 The absence of state protection is established on a balance of probabilities by means of clear and convincing evidence that the refugee protection claimant's country of origin is unable or unwilling to provide adequate-not perfect-protection.31 Additionally, in assessing whether state protection is adequate, a decision-maker must examine the actual operational adequacy of the state's actions, rather than its efforts to protect its citizens.32

Thus, to determine whether protection is adequate, it is important to analyze not only whether there are legislative and procedural frameworks in the country of reference, but also whether the state, through the police or other authorities, is actually prepared to operationally implement those frameworks. I must therefore have relevant, reliable and convincing evidence establishing that, on a balance of probabilities, the state protection is inadequate.33

Although I do not share the RPD's view concerning the appellants' unsuccessful attempt to file a complaint, I consider its conclusion correct. The appellants did not rebut Colombian state protection with clear and convincing evidence.
The RPD stated in its reasons that the female appellant did not have a profile that would lead to the entire state's refusal to assist her; however, it did not specify the nature of the profile.

The female appellant alleges that she has been threatened since XXXX 2019. Contrary to her BOC Form, in which she states that she XXXX several XXXX, the female appellant testified that she XXXX with and XXXX three XXXX by passing information to them so that they could conduct their investigation into corruption in the health and education systems.34 She therefore did not personally do any research or publish reports or articles on the topic. Instead, the female appellant played a secondary role, as an XXXX, not a primary role.

The appellants filed in evidence news articles35 describing the corruption in law enforcement in Colombia, particularly in Medellín, Bogotá and the Chocó area. One of those articles shows that the current government takes corruption issues very seriously and is considering a significant reform to combat corruption.36

However, the female appellant did not present any evidence of the results of what she reported or her collaboration with the journalists. She therefore did not show that she had had any impact on the corrupt activities in the education and health sectors. In that context, I agree with the RPD that it is unlikely that the politicians the female appellant fears will use their influence with the police against her.

In addition, the main profiles targeted in Colombia are social or community leaders who, among other things, denounce the presence of armed groups or participate in politics,37 which is not the case with the female appellant. While evidence of police corruption was filed on the record,38 that evidence does not describe cases similar to that of the female appellant, who took part in an investigative report on corruption. This therefore leads me to conclude that the evidence on the record does not establish that because of police corruption, the appellants could not obtain protection from the threats received.

At the hearing, the female appellant stated that she feared certain politicians and the paramilitary group Autodefensas Unidas de Colombia (United Self-Defence Forces of Colombia), although that was not included in her BOC Form. In that context, I note that the Victims and Land Restitution Law (LVRT) was passed in 2011 to provide assistance and reparation to those who, individually or collectively, were victims of the armed conflict. The LVRT covers, among others, those who are victims of threats.

Colombia is one of the oldest democracies in Latin America but has a history of widespread violence and serious human rights abuses.39 In that respect, the government has taken several measures to combat armed groups and corruption in the country. For instance, the Colombian government has deployed thousands of troops to combat armed groups, resulting in several losses for armed groups and weapons seizures.40 The documentary evidence41 reports that in 2018, there was an increase in homicides against social leaders and aggressions against ex-combatants, but that forced disappearances and kidnappings have decreased over the years. In addition, the number of people registered as victims in 2018 in the Registry of Victims has reached an all-time low since 1994.42

Between 2014 and 2017, the Colombian government invested over C$800 million to provide emergency humanitarian assistance to low-income victims of forced displacement.43 Although those resources are insufficient, improvements are noted in the victim assistance program.

The National Protection Unit was created in 2011 to provide protection to individuals, groups or communities who are at risk as a direct consequence of their activities or political, public, social or humanitarian roles.44 Although this program has suffered many setbacks and is criticized for its ineffectiveness and the slow implementation of protective measures,45 since its introduction, it has nonetheless provided protection to hundreds of individuals, including defenders of human rights, mayors, governors, judges, etc.46

I agree that the measures taken by the Colombian state have shortcomings and issues with effectiveness; however, considering the evidence on the record, I conclude that the appellants have failed to establish, on a balance of probabilities, the absence of state protection.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the RPD's determination that the appellants, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX, are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.
